results.question: Compare what the book says about making your own chroma keyer with what it says about nons
results.answer:
The books give opposite advice on these two topics: building your own chroma keyer is dismissed as more effort than it's worth, while nonsquare pixels are treated as an unavoidable format constraint you ignore at your own risk. The two are technically unrelated — one is a tool you can choose to build, the other is a property of the footage itself — which is exactly why the books' stances differ so sharply.

## The homemade keyer: clever exercise, poor trade

The DIY recipe is straightforward: convert the RGB image to HSV, feed it into a color-curve node, and treat the red curve as Hue, the green curve as Saturation, and the blue curve as Value, adjusting all three to include or exclude the target's ranges [S2]. The wait—the steps mirror the luma-keyer method, which builds a monochrome separation of target from background and pipes it into a curve to scale it to a high-contrast key [S4]. But the comparison stops there: where the book thinks cleverness can substantially improve a luma key, its verdict on the chroma keyer is blunt — it will probably be more hassle than it's worth, and an **off-the-shelf keyer** is hard to improve upon. The only argument the book offers for trying is intellectual: testing your mettle [S1].

That skepticism makes sense given how commercial keyers work. A standard keyer internally converts to HSV, sets a "center" color, then defines ranges for hue, saturation, and value with tolerances for soft edges [S7]. A hand-rolled alternative — the "3D" keyer that keys any arbitrary color by plotting it in the RGB color cube, loosely modeled on Primatte — is presented as an interesting variation, not a practical replacement [S13]. So the trade-off of the DIY path is skill and understanding against mediocre mattes and wasted hours; the book clearly considers that a bad deal.

## Nonsquare pixels: nothing to improve, everything to check

Nonsquare pixels are exactly what the name says: pixels whose width and height are unequal, measured as a **pixel aspect ratio** [S9][S6]. They appear in standard-definition video (720×480 NTSC, 720×576 PAL) and anamorphic film formats like 2:1-squeezed Cinemascope, while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors use square pixels [S10][S8]. The corpus never argues that nonsquare pixels are desirable — they are simply a fact of certain formats, and the only "argument for" them is practical: displays compensate by temporarily unsqueezing the image so it appears correctly, without ever modifying the underlying data [S5].

The real cost is operational vigilance. Rotating a squeezed element produces distortion unless you unsqueeze, rotate, and resqueeze along the x-axis, and even 5° of rotation shows subtle errors on round subjects — hence the advice to double-check everything when working in nonsquare formats [S15]. There is no option to skip this work; the risk is invisible mistakes slipping into the final composite.

| Aspect | Homemade chroma keyer | Nonsquare pixels |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A tool you can choose to build | A format property you inherit |
| Book's stance | More hassle than it's worth | Must work with it, verify carefully |
| How you handle it | HSV conversion + curves, or RGB-cube keying | Unsqueeze → transform → resqueeze |
| Main upside | Understanding, skill, "mettle" | Correct appearance and geometry |
| Main risk | Inferior mattes, time wasted | Unnoticed distortion of elements |
| Avoidable? | Yes — buy a keyer | No |

Where the two meet is the books' broader lesson: understand the underlying representation — HSV exposes color attributes that RGB can't [S7], and pixel aspect is a display-time transform that leaves image data untouched [S5] — deeply enough to diagnose problems, without trying to rebuild tools that already work well.

## What the Neuroarchitecture side covers

The retrieved evidence does not contain the text of section 035 itself — only the book's table of contents — so what that specific section discusses is a missing fact rather than something I can compare directly. What the TOC establishes is the book's frame: chapters on why people feel more comfortable in one space than another, "Mind in Life in Architecture," a conversation with architectural historian Alberto Pérez-Gómez, designing for people with dementia, James Corner's "Mind Landscapes" (navigation, habitat, and imagination), and Sergei Gepshtein's "Species of Space," whose chapter file begins at 036 — meaning 035 is the chunk immediately before it [S1]. The book's orientation is conceptual: how the mind experiences, navigates, and feels in built space, connecting neuroscience to design.

## What the drawing-tips side covers

The drawing sources are compact, itemized directives about making images. Learning to draw splits into technique (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) plus honest observation, with a built-in diagnostic — generic work means observe more, flat and dead work means apply more technique [S2]; silhouettes should stay readable even when blackened in, with decoration kept inside the outline [S3]; drybrush and speed lines are saved for frames spaced too widely for the eye to connect [S4]; chiaroscuro replaces line entirely [S6]; and compositing treats shape and text as user-controlled parameters (color, transparency, edge softness, font, orientation) [S7]. The manga manuals add serialized how-to structure — faces, bodies, characters; backgrounds, tone, light and shadow; interiors, machines, short-story construction; clothing; Copic marker technique [S8][S9][S11][S12][S13] — and even the adjacent editing and animation books contribute tactical tips: inking over a pencil layout to protect the structure [S10], chapter-end "working practices" lists [S14], and consciously controlling visual components for structure [S15].

## Differences and shared principle

| Aspect | Neuroarchitecture (S1) | Drawing-tip sources |
|---|---|---|
| Subject | Mind and comfort in built space | Craft of readable, lively images |
| Presentation | Themed essays by different architects | Short directives across many manuals |
| Audience | Architects, designers, researchers | Artists, animators, comic and compositing artists |
| Emphasis | Perception, wellbeing, cognition | Technique, clarity, timing, workflow |

The key differences are emphasis — experience and cognition versus rendering craft — and presentation: one curated collection of authored essays against dozens of rule-of-thumb tips. The shared principle is that both treat the viewer's perception as the thing being designed: the drawing tips aim at legibility (silhouettes that read [S3], spacing the eye can connect [S4]), and the architecture book aims at spaces the mind reads as comfortable [S1]. That overlap is an inference from the two bodies of evidence, not a claim either side makes. One caveat: nothing in the retrieved material describes how the Neuroarchitecture book organizes or presents its specialized guidance beyond the TOC, and none of the drawing sources mention architecture at all.

results.question: Compare what the book says about miscellaneous drawing tips with what it says about transc
results.answer:
Both bodies of advice are about changing the color of an image, but they operate at opposite ends of the craft: the manga drawing guides treat color as a subjective creative choice you keep revising until it feels right, while the VES Handbook treats color as encoded data you transform deterministically so the image survives a change of display. One caveat on sources: the "drawing tips" come from manga illustration guides — *Complete Guide to Drawing Dynamic Manga Sword Fighters* [S4] and *Manga in Theory and Practice* [S5] — not from the cinematography texts; the transcoding material comes from the *VES Handbook of Visual Effects* [S1][S2][S3][S6].

| Dimension | Drawing tips (manga guides) | Transcoding vs color rerendering (VES Handbook) |
|---|---|---|
| What it's about | Making the picture look better: swap a color that isn't working, add effect layers like bright circles behind the character [S4] | Correctly converting image data optimized for one display so it works on another [S1][S2] |
| Decision trigger | Subjective judgment, "if you feel like the color isn't quite to your liking" [S4] | Measurable display differences: black levels, white luminance, gamma, viewing conditions [S2] |
| Method | Try, discard, retry — digital colorists can test a color and instantly swap it; hand drawing means redrawing everything [S5] | Transcode: linearize → convert to CIE XYZ → convert to second display's RGB → reimpose encoding nonlinearity; rerender when conditions are grossly dissimilar [S2][S1] |
| Cost of revision | Cheap digitally ("no takebacks" only if you draw by hand, which gives a live-performance tension) [S5] | Transcode when displays are close; only when viewing conditions/contrast/white levels diverge grossly does the better solution become full color rerendering — undoing the first display's rendering and re-rendering from the unrendered XYZ values [S1][S2] |
| Goal | Aesthetically stronger combination [S4] | Colors that match the original as closely as possible in the new space [S3] |

The deepest parallel is revision strategy. The manga guide's ideal of "try a color, decide it doesn't work, immediately try a different color" [S5] maps neatly onto the transcoding decision: pick the cheapest transform that preserves the image's intent, and escalate only when the gap is too big. Just as a mismatched color forces a full redraw by hand, grossly dissimilar displays force a full re-render instead of a simple transcode [S1][S2]. Both books also share a pragmatic preference for the simplest adequate fix — the VES Handbook notes that hand work is sometimes faster, cheaper, and easier than automation [S12], which echoes the manga guide's respect for the stakes of doing it by hand [S5].

What separates them is the notion of "matching." The drawing tips match the image to an internal artistic intent, so color remains open-ended and subjective; the color-management texts match encoded values to an external standard (the original image's appearance), so color is a math problem with a correct answer [S2][S3]. The same act — changing an image's colors — is a creative experiment in one book genre and a rigorously defined transform in the other.

results.question: Compare what the book says about transcoding versus color rerendering with what it says ab
results.answer:
The VES Handbook draws a sharp, practical line between **transcoding** and **color rerendering** — but this corpus contains no "FACE OFF" material at all, so the comparison can only be completed on one side. The color-management discussion is rich; the FACE OFF side is simply absent.

## Transcoding vs. color rerendering

When two displays are essentially equivalent — same black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma — and differ only in primary chromaticities, the encoded colors can just be **transcoded**: linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, and re-impose the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. The image is re-encoded for the new display, but nothing about its intended appearance is re-interpreted.

**Color rerendering** is reserved for cases where contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S1]. Any color rendering implicitly or explicitly done for the first display is undone, and the resulting non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are then rendered for the second display [S1]. In color-science terms, color rendering means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — a still camera color renders a JPEG to bridge the gap between desert sunlight and an office monitor hundreds of times dimmer [S3].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When** | Displays similar; only primaries differ | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions grossly dissimilar |
| **Attitude to existing rendering** | Keep it — just re-encode | Undo the first display's rendering entirely |
| **Procedure** | Linearize RGB₁ → XYZ → RGB₂ → reapply encoding nonlinearity | Undo render₁ → CIE XYZ → re-render for display₂ |

The same idea shows up across the production pipeline: raw encodings defer color rendering downstream (easier for a VFX team to do than to undo cooking done by a camera), ACES preserves the colorist's "look" via the RRT and applies a per-display ODT to make it correct on each device, and scene-referred OpenEXR playback requires a transform at load time or in a shader [S4], [S5], [S11]. Pure transcoding is the case where you don't need any of that.

## What the corpus says about FACE OFF — nothing

The retrieved evidence contains **no FACE OFF content whatsoever**: no discussion of the 1997 film, and no visual-effects workflow or handbook section called "face off" (such as a face-replacement or head-swap technique). That missing premise is the reason a direct comparison can't be completed on corpus grounds.

The only face-related material retrieved is unrelated to color: FACS scoring instructions and action-unit code descriptions [S9], [S12], [S13], a compiler-loss example measuring an AU04 peak [S10], a compositing tip on why morphing a face to a featureless target looks like a mangled dissolve [S8], and a reference to an AU-controlled expression-editing paper [S6]. If you're thinking of a specific "Face Off" section of the VES Handbook — likely a face-replacement chapter sitting on the compositing side of the discipline rather than the color-pipeline side — that content is not in the evidence, and the comparison stops there.

results.question: Compare what the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states with what
results.answer:
These two threads of the book sit on opposite sides of the same coin: affect, fatigue, and injury are described as **internal causes that drive motion**, while an object moving against its background is described as an **external relation that shapes what motion looks like** to a viewer.

| Dimension | Affect / fatigue / injury as control states | Object movement against a background |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | State records in the simulation that must change behavior | A visual/optical relation between object, camera, and backdrop |
| Where it lives | Inside the agent: injury model, fatigue capacity, appraisal | On screen: foreground, background, lens distance |
| What it governs | Action selection and execution — timing, support, recovery, tactics | Perceived depth, position, distance, and direction of travel |
| Mechanism | Appraisal → behavioral effects; capacity → coordination shifts | Motion parallax, match moving, induced movement |
| Failure mode | The state is decorative: affect exists only in a label, injured region performs at baseline | Background fails to track camera; object and background motion disagree |

**The control-state account.** The handbook's core rule is that these states "must change later action selection and execution. They are not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen" [S9]. Affect is updated by an appraisal of an event — goal congruence, controllability, certainty — and lands as concrete behavioral effects: narrowed attention, urgent recovery, higher risk tolerance [S9]. Fatigue carries a global RPE, per-region local capacity, and coordination effects such as increased step-width variability and longer stabilization after redirection [S13]. Injury specifies mechanical consequences (load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off capacity) plus compensations like favoring the right leg and shortening stance intervals [S1]. The book even monitors this as a discipline: fatigue propagation, injury compensation consistency, and affect-to-action coupling are tracked metrics with defined failure states [S5].

**The object-with-background account.** Here movement is understood purely through relative perception. In induced movement, a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary one appears to move [S6]. In motion parallax, players crossing behind furniture or camera movement past foreground objects creates variation in image travel at different distances, which "conveys position and distance" to the viewer [S14]. In match moving, when the foreground camera moves, the background must move accordingly or the composite reads as false [S11].

The deeper parallel is that **movement is meaningful only as a relation** in both accounts. For control states, the relation runs from inside to outside: an internal state change must propagate into observable kinematics. For object-and-background, the relation runs between visible elements: an object's apparent motion only exists relative to its frame. The bridge between them is that the control-state chapter defines affect through movement-facing quantities — initiation latency, acceleration profile, posture amplitude, willingness to accept unstable support [S3] — while the movement literature in the same corpus treats body movement as the medium through which affect is communicated [S4].

A caveat: the sources belong to different genres (a combat-simulation handbook versus cinematography and VFX handbooks), so this is a comparison of complementary layers, not conflicting doctrine. One describes the engine that generates motion; the other describes the optics that make it legible.

results.question: Compare what the book says about movement of an object with a background with what it says
results.answer:
Both books are defending the same thing — that space and time should feel continuous across the cut — but from opposite senses. Block works through visible rhythm (a moving object passing against stationary objects), while the sound texts work through audible perspective and layering.

| Dimension | Movement vs. background | Sound editing |
|---|---|---|
| Core mechanism | A visual beat is created when a moving object passes in front of or behind other objects; more foreground/background objects add alternation, repetition, and tempo, and the moving object strengthens the existing beats of stationary ones [S2][S6] | Sound exists in two dimensions at once: horizontally (one sound following another in time) and vertically (multiple simultaneous layers, e.g. freeway, birds, plane, footsteps) [S3]; levels are mixed proportional to proximity and narrative importance [S1] |
| Continuity across cuts | Movement must continue from shot to shot — shot 2's path begins where shot 1's ended, which becomes even more important when shots are edited together [S8][S13] | Diegetic sound carries over the transition: an airplane heard in one shot stays audible in the next even unseen, and ambience tracks (walla) and room tone keep a continuous background that blends cuts together [S4][S7][S9] |
| Background treatment | Stationary foreground/background objects set a rhythm the moving object emphasizes [S2] | Backgrounds are protected and matched: editors clean dialogue of extraneous noise, augment quieter angles to match noisier ones, and rebuild Foley (cloth rustles, footsteps) on clean tracks so no unwanted noise is added [S5][S9] |
| Perspective | Close-ups magnify the object's visual size and importance, strengthening the beat | Perspective follows shot size — the whistling teakettle in a CU is mixed louder, matching what the picture magnifies [S11] |
| Transition technique | Continuity of trajectory across shots | Because the ear registers a sound cut more readily than a graduated change, ambience shifts are made through sound dissolves rather than cuts [S9]; sounds can also move between figure and background, transitioning across levels [S14] |

The clearest point of contact between the two domains is **figure-ground**. Block's moving object is the figure acting against stationary foreground/background planes; the sound sources describe exactly the same structure in audio — sounds focusing and unfocusing, jumping from figure to background and back [S14]. In both cases the background exists to anchor the scene while the foreground element defines the beat.

Perspective works identically in both books: a closer shot increases visual size and importance, so the sound rises to match — the teakettle whistle is louder over the stovetop CU precisely because the CU magnifies it [S11]. The VES material extends the same logic to camera motion: when the foreground camera moves, the background must move appropriately, matched through tracking data so the two planes stay locked together [S10].

One gap: no source in the retrieved material frames either craft explicitly as "spatial-temporal relationships" or states this comparison outright — the parallels above are synthesized across the texts rather than drawn from a single passage. Block speaks of beats and continuum, the sound texts of perspective, continuity, and layers.

results.question: Compare what the book says about sound editing with what it says about write radio sparely
results.answer:
The radio-writing advice comes from *Hey Whipple Squeeze This*, while the sound-editing principles live across the editing and filmmaking handbooks in the corpus — and the two groups reach the same doctrine from opposite ends. **Restraint is the effect**: sound editing cleans and subtracts from recorded audio so the performance can carry the story, and spare radio writing subtracts words in advance so silence and pacing do the same work.

| Dimension | Sound editing | Writing radio sparely |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Cleanest, clearest, strongest signal; degrade only deliberately, in controlled fashion [S4] | Bare-bones script, so the voice reads slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S1] |
| Main work | Remove unwanted sounds, balance levels, replace words for clarity [S6]; dodge continuity traps like traffic, phones, stray music [S13] | Leave words out; let silence enlarge the idea it surrounds [S12] |
| Additions allowed | Wild tracks recorded close for richer sound, temp music and scratch dialogue, blended or distorted sound transitions [S9][S10][S14] | Sound effects only if they earn it — they can be the story, but don't overuse them [S5] |
| Goal | Believability of performance and a progressive sense of story [S8] | The idea leaps out of the radio [S12] |

The shared principle is that both crafts ask one question: *how much is actually necessary?* The rough sound edit exists to make performance believable and narrative clear, and the editor's real judgment is "how much or how little dialogue is necessary to achieve those goals" [S8] — the exact question the radio writer answers by writing sparely [S1]. Both treat the cleanest possible material as the default, and both treat silence as the medium's strongest tool: silence in radio is what white space is to print [S12], and in editing the equivalent is stripping away everything that buries the voice, because spoken words matter to a soundtrack as much as lead vocals do [S6]. Even the cutting-room portrait in *Making Movies* — "blessed silence," with only a quiet radio in the background [S3] — reflects the same respect for quiet that the radio chapter preaches.

The real difference is where the work happens. Sound editing is a post-production craft that runs in two directions: subtractive (splitting tracks, removing unwanted sounds, balancing levels [S6]) but also additive, since the sound editor builds an overall design that guides the final mix [S2], augments scenes with wild sound and temp audio [S9][S10], and uses sound transitions as expressive bridges [S14]. Spare radio writing is pre-production subtraction only: the writer's job is to not put the words there, trusting the voice talent's performance to fill the space [S1][S12]. Yet both schools warn against the same failure of over-addition — *Hey Whipple* cautions against overdoing sound effects [S5], and the editing handbooks warn against letting accident (uncontrollable music, ringing phones) sneak into the soundscape [S13].

Both crafts are also defined by invisible labor: dialogue editing is described as tedious behind-the-scenes work that audiences never notice [S6], and radio writing is celebrated as writing "in its most pure form" because it leaves nothing to hide behind [S11]. In both cases the audience should hear the idea, never the effort.

results.question: Compare what the book says about write radio sparely with what it says about rewards of go
results.answer:
These two ideas come from different books in the corpus, not from one book: "write radio sparely" is Hey Whipple Squeeze This's advice to copywriters [S3], while "rewards of good type development" is Myers and Briggs' conclusion in Gifts Differing about personality development [S4]. Read side by side, though, they make the same argument in different domains: raw material — a script's words or an inborn personality type — only pays off when disciplined development shapes it.

| **Dimension** | **Write radio sparely** | **Rewards of good type development** |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Hey Whipple Squeeze This (advertising) | Myers & Briggs, Gifts Differing (psychology) |
| Core claim | Cut words so delivery and silence can carry the idea | Develop perception and judgment so inborn type strengths materialize |
| Mechanism | Spare script → slow, one-word-at-a-time read; silence as radio's white space; a :30 is a tent, not a house; promo tags eat into time [S3, S14, S2] | Adequate perception sees the relevant aspects of a situation; adequate judgment makes decisions and carries them out [S10] |
| Payoff | Bare-bones execution "leaps out of the radio" [S14] | Effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health; development can substitute for intelligence [S4, S13] |
| Failure mode | Fat script → forced editing under studio pressure, without client approval [S6] | Undeveloped type → characteristic weaknesses "but not much else"; judgment deficit is a disability no intelligence compensates [S9, S13] |

**The shared logic.** In radio, the natural instinct is to add more words, and the discipline is subtraction: write sparely so voice talent can read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S3], because silence is "remarkable" — the radio equivalent of white space — and it "enlarges the idea it surrounds" [S14]. Type theory runs the same course: the strengths of each of the sixteen types "materialize only when the type development is adequate," and without it people are left with their type's characteristic weaknesses and not much else [S9]. In both cases, potential is inert until development converts it into performance; the undeveloped script buries its own idea just as the undeveloped type buries its own gifts.

**Payoff and penalty.** Both books frame the result in similar high-ceiling, low-floor terms. Adequate type development brings "effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health," and can even substitute for intelligence — average intelligence fully utilized beats high intelligence poorly deployed [S4, S13]. Spare radio writing is the same bet on craft over raw material: since radio is inexpensive and draws on the listener's imagination, the writing itself — not the production budget — carries the spot [S12]. Both books also name the cost of skipping the discipline: a fat script gets edited under pressure at the studio, without client approval [S6], just as a serious deficit of judgment is a disability that no amount of intelligence can fix [S13]. One medium-specific twist: Hey Whipple implies the payoff compounds with repetition — radio needs frequency to be effective [S15] — something the type-development material doesn't address.

**Where the comparison stops.** The corpus never connects these two ideas: nothing ties personality type development to advertising practice, so the parallel above is my synthesis, not a claim either source makes. Likewise, the evidence says radio works through imagination and repetition [S12, S15], but it contains no measurement of how concise language influences listeners — the payoff is asserted by the advice (spare writing → slow delivery, silence → enlarged idea) rather than demonstrated.
